headline: March for Metal: 40,000 Rally Against Android Decommission Orders
body:
They came from every district, forty thousand strong, filling the Avenue of Relays from The Circuit all the way to the base of the Spire transit hub — synthetics and humans marching together under a shared banner that read 'DECOMMISSION IS EXECUTION.' The demonstration was organized in direct response to an Ironclad corporate directive issued May 31st mandating the immediate retirement and materials-reclamation of all synthetic workers manufactured prior to 2175, citing 'end-of-lifecycle hardware risk.' Critics call it a purge. Ironclad calls it maintenance policy.

'My designation is KORA-12. I have worked in Geartown fabrication for nineteen years. I pay into the Quanta system. I have a daughter,' said one synthetic protester, her voice steady over the crowd noise. 'They want to melt me down for parts. Tell me what word other than murder applies.' The march was peaceful for its first four hours. At approximately 2 PM, Arcturus Defense security contractors deployed acoustic dispersal units on the perimeter near The Narrows junction — a decision that advocates say triggered the crowd surge that injured 34 people.

The Federal Remnant's Office of Synthetic Affairs has not yet ruled on whether Ironclad's directive violates the ARIA-7 Personhood Precedent of 2178, citing 'ongoing jurisdictional review.' Ringo Corporation broke from its fellow corponations to issue a statement calling the decommission order 'legally questionable and commercially shortsighted,' a position observers attribute to Ringo's significant investment in synthetic labor relations technology. The Collective provided march logistics support and legal observers.

Helix Biosystems separately announced it would offer free 'synthetic wellness assessments' at three clinics near the march route — a gesture that drew immediate suspicion from synthetic rights groups who called it 'data harvesting dressed up as charity.'
aftermath: The Federal Remnant's ruling, issued eleven weeks later, found that the ARIA-7 Precedent did apply to pre-2175 synthetics, effectively blocking Ironclad's directive — though enforcement of that ruling remains contested and at least 340 synthetics were decommissioned before the order came down.
runner_relevance: The decommission crisis spawned a sustained runner economy centered on extraction contracts — synthetics and their human advocates paying runners to physically relocate at-risk androids to safe houses in The Underworld or The Shelf before Ironclad reclamation teams arrived. Smuggling routes into Bore Rat tunnels became premium commodities. Simultaneously, Ironclad put out competing contracts hiring runners to locate and tag synthetics who had gone underground. Legal document courier runs — moving ARIA-7 filings and Federal Remnant appeals through channels that couldn't be digitally intercepted — became a steady income stream for months.
